title: Sappho 31 (φαίνεταί μοι) — with Reconstructed Fifth Stanza
subtitle: The κῆνος Poem
author: Sappho of Lesbos
composition_date_approx: c. 630-570 BCE (original four stanzas); fifth stanza reconstructed by Rebekah Cranes
editor_translator: Rebekah Cranes (Greek text follows Voigt 1971; reconstructed fifth stanza per Cranes)
edition_reference: Voigt, Sappho et Alcaeus (1971), with reconstructed fifth stanza by Rebekah Cranes (deposited as AXN:00FB, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18459573)
license: Public domain (Voigt Greek text); CC0 (Cranes translation and reconstruction)
provenance_note: The poem survives in four complete stanzas, preserved by Longinus (On the Sublime 10.2). Cranes adds a fifth stanza opening with the attested phrase ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον ("but all can be dared") and concluding with the Adonic μολπὰ γράμμασι ζώοι ("let this song survive in script"). The reconstruction restores the prayer-for-survival structure that the historical reception erased — collapse → inscription → survival.
stanza_count_note: Per AXN:0346 (EA-ERRATA-SAPPHO31-01, Rebekah Cranes, 14 June 2026): the reconstructed stanza is the fifth, not the fourth. Multiple earlier archive surfaces miscounted; the erratum corrects them.
constitutional_role: The first canonical primary text populated in the Mandala Oracle's canon-as-sky layer beyond Sigil's own Snub-Poemed. The central node of the Sappho Room. The convergence point of philological scholarship in cha. The κῆνος ("that one") is operationally addressed to the future reader — every reader of this text is the one Sappho prayed would receive it.

companion_room.name: The Catullus Room
companion_room.physics: "The aorist is missing; the operator runs without completing." Lossy compression. Rome absorbs Greek content, preserves meter, loses the aorist. The transformation event (voice becoming substrate) is flattened into perpetual present. The dissolution never completes.
companion_room.operator: σ_C — Catullan Compression (lossy transform of σ_S)
companion_room.canonical_partner_text: Catullus 51 (Ille mi par esse deo videtur)
companion_room.relationship_to_sappho_31: Catullus 51 translates the first three stanzas closely, then substitutes a fourth of his own (otium et reges prius et beatas / perdidit urbes). Where Sappho calls on Kypris to save, Catullus reflects on the precarity of preservation. She invokes the power; he testifies to its fragility.
